Western Digital officially announced price increases across its entire mechanical hard drive product line, with delivery times extended by 6-10 weeks. Market conditions saw queues forming at hard drive factories for bulk purchases, and terminal prices for some HDD models nearly doubled. For sectors requiring long-term video storage, such as public security, transportation, finance, and education, this was not just a matter of "hard drives getting more expensive." On one hand, regulatory requirements extended video surveillance retention periods from 30 to 90 days for key locations like banks, large event venues, airports, and train stations. On the other, the shift to 4MP and 6MP ultra-high-definition cameras increased storage demands. The price hikes doubled corporate storage costs, leaving expansion plans in a dilemma. Zhongke Tongliang Jingang V high-throughput intelligent video storage products, leveraging industry-leading chip-level lossless video compression and efficient storage capabilities, emerged as a key solution to counter the price surge. Without altering video quality or affecting AI analysis, they enable more content in the same storage space, saving businesses on new drive purchases, data center electricity, and maintenance costs, addressing the industry's challenges of insufficient storage and high additional expenses.

excerpt_i18n.en: Nvidia is once again at the center of attention. Within just a few days, two seemingly unrelated events have dominated headlines: a live discussion between Stanford professor Fei-Fei Li and Nvidia's chief scientist Jim Fan on the topic of "enabling AI to act in the world," and the first public appearance of Madison Huang, daughter of Jensen Huang and senior director of product marketing at Nvidia, who engaged in a dialogue with Xie Chen, founder of Lightwheel, exploring the future of simulation, embodied intelligence, and Sim2Real. One event represents the academic sphere, while the other showcases the future leaders of the industry. When viewed together, they reveal a common narrative: Nvidia is aggressively advancing its simulation computing strategy. Jensen Huang has set this as the direction for the next decade, using three pillars—Omniverse, Isaac Sim, and Physical AI—to build a "smart physical world computing network" that bridges the virtual and real worlds. In essence, Nvidia aims not just to create more powerful computing capabilities but to develop a system that allows AI to "learn and act in the world," enabling machines not only to understand data but to truly comprehend the world itself. Nvidia is playing a long game. A new landscape of three "computers" has emerged, and over the past decade, Nvidia has quietly transformed from a graphics card manufacturer into an AI-focused entity.

Today's Headlines:
Absurd! An automaker trials two-shift system in R&D, programmers now work night shifts.
Recently, an internal email screenshot labeled "D Project Two-Shift Implementation Plan Review Meeting" went viral on social platforms. The email revealed that an automaker held a review meeting on October 11, 2025, deciding to pilot T and T projects with a "dual-shift system" to compress development cycles, aiming to complete a traditionally 20+ month vehicle R&D process within 12 months.
Meeting notes listed four core bottlenecks: high difficulty in ADAS hardware-software integration, unlocked performance platform solutions, long data release and physical conversion cycles, and delayed prototype deliveries. To address these, the factory requires night shifts for CAE simulation, crash testing, road testing, and data calibration, while coordinating supplier support.
